architectural_implications.after: Agent resources live in version control and are applied via pipeline, with diffs, reviews, and rollbacks.
architectural_implications.before: Agent prompts and long-term resources configured manually, out-of-band, or per-environment in console/UI.
architectural_implications.consequence: Agent changes become reviewable in PRs and reproducible across environments, but require disciplined repo structure and sync tooling.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent configuration is managed as declarative YAML in a repo and synced by CI/CD via ant-cli.

architectural_implications.after: Tenant isolation is a platform-level namespace construct; one workspace per customer where strict segregation is required.
architectural_implications.before: Multi-tenant isolation handled in application logic (filtering, row-level checks).
architectural_implications.consequence: Stronger security guarantees but proliferation of workspaces and duplicated shared resources; no cross-workspace access ('tunneling').
architectural_implications.observation: Isolation is enforced at the workspace/organization boundary, with API keys scoped to a workspace.

architectural_implications.after: The agent loop can be pointed at a self-hosted sandbox to obtain GPU or high-memory compute.
architectural_implications.before: All agent execution runs in the platform's default sandbox with its fixed resource profile.
architectural_implications.consequence: Teams can scale compute-heavy agents beyond platform limits, at the cost of operating their own sandbox infrastructure.
architectural_implications.observation: Execution sandbox becomes pluggable (self-hosted providers like Modal) while the agent loop remains managed.

core_insights.why_it_matters: Isolation is enforced at the platform boundary rather than in application code, which is a stronger security guarantee but also a hard partitioning constraint that forces duplication of shared resources across tenants.

core_insights.insight: Evaluation is run as a continuous cloud harness that is updated in lockstep with new model releases: Anthropic accesses models early specifically to revise harness assumptions, and scales eval by spinning up ~10,000 parallel cloud sessions against diverse data. This implies the harness itself is a maintained artifact, not a fixed benchmark.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Treating the eval harness as a versioned, continuously-updated component (rather than a static test suite) is what prevents stale assumptions from silently invalidating results after model updates.

core_insights.generalization: Pluggable execution backends are the standard escape hatch for managed agent platforms whose default compute tier is insufficient.
core_insights.insight: The managed sandbox has bounded compute, so GPU or high-memory workloads are handled by substituting a self-hosted sandbox (e.g., Modal) that runs the agent loop, with Anthropic providing cookbooks for third-party sandbox integrations. This implies the agent loop and the execution sandbox are separable layers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Defines the abstraction boundary: orchestration/agent logic stays platform-managed while the execution environment becomes pluggable, giving teams a path to custom hardware without abandoning the managed control plane.

core_insights.generalization: Long-running agent tasks fare better under outcome-based termination (define success, let the agent iterate) than under fixed step budgets, and delegation to sub-sessions avoids blocking the coordinator.
core_insights.insight: The coordinator–subagent pattern keeps the main agent active while sub-agents run parallel subtasks across separate threads/sessions, with a session event stream API as the coordination substrate. summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Anthropic team members
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Advanced deployment, CI/CD integration, multi-tenancy, evals, and sandboxing for Claude Managed Agents
  • Purpose: Address developer inquiries and clarify advanced operational aspects of building, testing, evaluating, and scaling Claude Managed Agents. In this final Q&A session from the Claude Managed Agents workshop at the AI Engineer World's Fair, Anthropic engineers answer developer questions regarding agent CI/CD pipelines, evaluation strategies and quality best practices, multi-tenancy isolation options, compute resource allocation and GPU environments, and orchestrating sub-agents across long-running sessions.

Topic Map

CI/CD and Agent Workflow Updates

  • Explanation: How developers can version agent definitions, prompt Yamls, and long-term resources in codebases and automatically update deployments via CLI tools.
  • Key claims:
    • Ant-CLI wraps Anthropic APIs to allow Terraform-like YAML configuration of agent resources.
    • CI/CD pipelines can automatically push updates whenever code repo resources change.
  • Examples:
    • Storing agent long-term resources in YAML within a codebase and syncing via CI/CD.
  • Terminology:
    • ant-cli
    • CI/CD
    • Terraform-like YAML
  • Why it matters: Enables automated, version-controlled agent management across engineering teams.

Evaluations Best Practices

  • Explanation: Approaches for running evals on new model releases and agent updates, highlighting the Garbage In, Garbage Out principle and iterative prompt tuning.
  • Key claims:
    • Anthropic runs continuous evals in cloud environments, accessing models early to update harness assumptions.
    • High-quality data is critical for accurate evaluation; poor benchmark design leads to uninformative metrics.
  • Examples:
    • Spinning up 10,000 parallel cloud sessions to evaluate prompts and assumptions against diverse data sets.
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • harness
    • garbage in garbage out
  • Why it matters: Ensures reliability and prevents degradation of agent performance during prompt or model updates.

Multi-Tenancy and Data Segregation

  • Explanation: Structuring workspaces, API keys, and organizations to maintain strict tenant isolation and compliance for enterprise customers.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are bound to workspaces; API keys within a workspace control resource access.
    • Workspace design or isolated organizations can achieve customer-level data segregation.
  • Examples:
    • Creating one workspace per customer to enforce strict data segregation.
  • Terminology:
    • workspace
    • organization
    • data segregation
    • multi-tenancy
  • Why it matters: Crucial for enterprise compliance and security when deploying shared agents across different clients.

Compute Environments, Memory, and GPUs

  • Explanation: Managing resource requirements like higher memory or GPU needs for agents using self-hosted sandboxes and integrations like Modal.
  • Key claims:
    • For custom resource allocations (GPUs or high memory), developers should use self-hosted sandboxes like Modal.
    • Anthropic provides cookbooks for first-party integrations with third-party sandbox providers.
  • Examples:
    • Hooking up Modal instances to run agent loops instead of default Anthropic sandboxes.
  • Terminology:
    • Modal
    • self-hosted sandboxes
    • cookbooks
  • Why it matters: Allows developers to scale compute-heavy agents beyond default platform constraints.

Long-Running Sessions and Coordinator Patterns

  • Explanation: Handling hours-long agent runs, tracking checkpoint status, and coordinating sub-agents without blocking the main thread.
  • Key claims:
    • Outcome-driven evaluation and exit criteria are best for very long tasks.
    • Coordinator-subagent patterns allow main agents to remain active while sub-agents execute parallel subtasks.
  • Examples:
    • Setting exit criteria for a task like 'rebuild blank' and letting Claude iterate until criteria are met.
  • Terminology:
    • coordinator pattern
    • sub-agents
    • exit criteria
    • session event stream
  • Why it matters: Enables robust execution of complex, multi-hour engineering tasks.

Key Points

CI/CD Integration for Agents

  • Explanation: Agent configurations can be treated like infrastructure-as-code using CLI wrappers.
  • Evidence: Mention of ant-cli and syncing YAML configurations on git push.
  • Practical implication: Teams can manage agent updates through standard pull request workflows.

Importance of Data Quality in Evals

  • Explanation: Evaluation quality depends entirely on the quality and specificity of the test data and prompts.
  • Evidence: Statement on garbage in, garbage out regarding initial evaluation assumptions.
  • Practical implication: Developers must invest time in refining historical sessions and scoring rubrics.

Workspace-Level Multi-Tenancy

  • Explanation: Isolation and access control are managed via workspaces and organization admin settings.
  • Evidence: Explanation that API keys are bound to workspaces and admin privileges govern resource partitioning.
  • Practical implication: Architecting customer-specific workspaces ensures data privacy.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Coordinator-Subagent Pattern

  • How it works: A main coordinator agent delegates work to multiple sub-agents running across separate threads or sessions, gathering tool results and maintaining a central chat interface.
  • Components:
    • Main coordinator agent
    • Sub-agents
    • Session event stream API
  • When to use: When building complex applications requiring parallel subtasks or role-based delegation.

Examples & Case Studies

A developer asked about maintaining tenant isolation across 100 enterprise customers.

  • Illustrates: Multi-tenancy and data segregation best practices using workspaces.
  • Lesson: Creating per-customer workspaces or using separate organizational units provides the necessary isolation.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Use ant-cli to manage agent definitions as code in YAML.
    • Leverage workspace structures for multi-tenant data separation.
  • Strategic:
    • Define clear exit criteria and outcome metrics for long-running agent tasks.
    • Integrate self-hosted providers like Modal when agents require GPU or high-memory compute.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How does fine-grained permission control evolve across larger enterprise workspaces?
    • What are the latency tradeoffs when scaling parallel sub-agent sessions?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • ant-cli allows Terraform-like YAML configuration for deploying agent resources (feature claim)
  • Self-hosted sandboxes like Modal can be integrated with Claude Managed Agents for GPU access (technical architecture claim)

Notable Quotes

"garbage in, garbage out" (at 6:47) "we don't have uh kind of tunneling today" (at 13:54)

Compressed Summary

  • Manage agent configurations via CLI and YAML version control
  • Ensure robust evaluation metrics with high-quality historical data
  • Achieve multi-tenant isolation using workspace and organization boundaries
  • Use Modal or custom sandboxes for GPU and high-memory workloads
  • Deploy coordinator-subagent patterns for long-running, multi-threaded tasks
  • Keywords: agents, cicd, evals, multitenancy, sandboxing
  • Core insight: Claude Managed Agents support enterprise-grade workflows through version-controlled YAML configuration, flexible workspace isolation, and scalable sandbox integrations.
